The following text is adapted from Richard Connell’s 1923 short story “The Man Who Could Imitate a Bee.”

An ornithologist is a scientist who studies birds. At twelve [years old Hervey Deyo] had resolved to be a scientist and furthermore a great scientist. He determined to pursue the career of ornithologist; there was something so dignified and withal scientific about a science that called the sparrow [i]Passer domesticus[/i] and the robin [i]Erithacus rubecula[/i]. He made rapid progress. On his thirteenth birthday he took a bird walk at dawn and was able to record in his note-book the scientific names of forty-nine birds, including the ruby-and-topaz humming-bird ([i]Chrysolampis mosquitus[/i]) which is rare in that part of the country.

questions.passage: The Bantu expansion refers to the gradual dispersal of Bantu-speaking peoples (which today include, among other groups, the Hlubi in South Africa and the Tutsi in Rwanda) and their languages from an ancestral homeland in West-Central Africa across much of sub-Saharan Africa over approximately 3,500 years, starting about 4,000–5,000 years ago (ya). Citing the discovery of grinding equipment dating as far back as 5,000 ya consistent with processing of plant foods, some researchers have asserted that the Bantu expansion can be explained by the farming/language dispersal hypothesis. This hypothesis proposes that the dispersal of many of the world’s large language families—for instance, Sino-Tibetan—was driven primarily by the adoption of agriculture.
questions.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly challenge the assertion about the Bantu expansion presented in the text?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The earliest unambiguous archaeobotanical evidence of plant cultivation and domestication in West-Central Africa consists of pearl millet ([i]Pennisetum glaucum[/i]) found in three sites in present-day Cameroon dated to around 2,200–2,350 ya and in one site in the present-day Democratic Republic of the Congo dated to around 2,200 ya.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reconstructed vocabulary from Proto-Bantu, the ancestral language from which all later Bantu languages descended, contains terms for some wild plant species that early Bantu speakers actively managed and cultivated but that were never fully domesticated into true crop plants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lexical reconstructions indicate that the earliest Bantu speakers’ words for yams, starchy tubers that are today an agricultural staple throughout sub-Saharan Africa, were inherited from languages predating the arrival of Bantu ancestral groups in their homeland.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Among the earliest archaeobotanical evidence of plant farming in East Africa, which Bantu-speaking peoples may have reached as early as 3,500 ya, are traces of cowpea ([i]Vigna unguiculata[/i]), a legume crop believed to have originated in West Africa, which were discovered in the Kakapel Rockshelter in present-day Kenya.

questions.passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

• The typical resting viscosity of oobleck (cornstarch mixed with water) is 5‑100 centipoise (cP).
• Oobleck increases in viscosity (becomes thicker) when stirred.
• The typical resting viscosity of fruit jam is 5,000‑10,000 (cP).
• Fruit jam decreases in viscosity (becomes thinner) when stirred.
• A fluid is Newtonian if its viscosity remains stable under shear (mechanical force such as being stirred or squeezed).
• A fluid is non‑Newtonian if its viscosity changes under shear.
questions.prompt: The student wants to contrast how shear affects fruit jam and oobleck. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Though the viscosities of both oobleck and fruit jam change under shear, oobleck's typical resting viscosity (5‑100 cP) is lower than that of fruit jam (5,000‑10,000 cP).

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fruit jam is non‑Newtonian, meaning its viscosity decreases under shear; oobleck, by contrast, increases in viscosity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fruit jam becomes thinner when stirred, while oobleck becomes thicker.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oobleck has a much lower resting viscosity than fruit jam but becomes thicker under shear.
